questions.q: Why is `.iterrows()` slow on a large DataFrame compared to a vectorized operation?
options: It sorts the DataFrame before iterating
It rebuilds a Series object and boxes values for every row, adding Python-level overhead per row
It only works on DataFrames with fewer than 1,000 rows
It copies the entire DataFrame to disk before iterating
questions.explain: `.iterrows()` constructs a new Series for each row and boxes each value, so the per-row Python overhead dominates runtime at scale, unlike vectorized operations that stay in compiled code.

questions.q: Which function is the vectorized equivalent of an if/elif/elif/else chain applied across a whole column?
options: np.select
df.iterrows()
df.apply(axis=1)
np.array_equal
questions.explain: `np.select` takes a list of condition arrays and a list of choices and evaluates each condition once across the full column, replacing a multi-branch if/elif chain.

questions.q: What does the `.str` accessor on a pandas Series provide?
options: A way to convert any Series to string dtype permanently
Vectorized string methods that run across the whole Series instead of looping element by element
A faster version of Python's built-in `str()` function
A method that only works on the DataFrame index, not columns
questions.explain: The `.str` accessor exposes string methods like `.strip()`, `.upper()`, and `.replace()` that apply across every element of the Series at once, avoiding a per-element Python loop.

questions.q: When combining two boolean masks in pandas, which operators should you use?
options: Python's `and` and `or` keywords
`&` and `|`, with parentheses around each comparison
`and=` and `or=`
questions.explain: Python's `and`/`or` only evaluate single truth values, not arrays. Boolean Series must be combined with `&` and `|`, and parentheses are needed because of operator precedence.

questions.q: According to this lesson, when is writing a genuine row-by-row loop still the right choice?
options: Whenever the DataFrame has more than one column
Never — vectorization always replaces loops
When each step depends on the previous computed result and no built-in (like cumsum, shift, or ewm) covers the pattern
Only when working with string data
questions.explain: Vectorization covers most cases, but genuinely stateful computations where each step depends on the prior computed result, and no built-in rolling/cumulative function covers it, are where a real loop (or later, a compiled one) is appropriate.
